name: Marxism–Leninism
info: Marxism–Leninism is a communist ideology built on Marx and Lenin and formulated under Stalin in the Soviet Union in the 1920s; it became the state ideology of the Soviet Union and of many communist states in the 20th century.

facts.thinkers: Vladimir Lenin, whose Bolshevism supplied its method of revolution; Joseph Stalin, who defined it and made it the Soviet orthodoxy; Karl Radek, who proposed the name Marxism–Leninism–Stalinism in 1934; Leon Trotsky, its leading critic from the left within the party; Mao Zedong, Josip Broz Tito and Enver Hoxha, who produced rival variants; Rosa Luxemburg, an early critic of the vanguard
facts.texts: Lenin's Imperialism, the Highest Stage of Capitalism (1917); Stalin's Concerning Questions of Leninism (1926), Dialectical and Historical Materialism and the textbook History of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union (Bolsheviks) (1938); Khrushchev's On the Cult of Personality and Its Consequences (25 February 1956)
facts.ideas: a two-stage revolution, socialism before communism; a vanguard party organised through democratic centralism; a one-party state; a planned economy with the means of production under state control; socialism in one country; dialectical and historical materialism; atheism; opposition to colonialism and imperialism
facts.today: the official ideology of the ruling parties of China, Cuba, Laos and Vietnam, and of Hoxhaist, Maoist and neo-Stalinist parties elsewhere; the state ideology of North Korea is derived from it; Maoist insurgencies continue in the Philippines, India and Turkey

t: Marxism–Leninism held that a vanguard party, organised through democratic centralism, would seize power for the proletariat and build a one-party state with a planned economy as the road to a classless, stateless society.

It was formulated after Lenin's death in 1924 by Stalin and his supporters, who set socialism in one country against Trotsky's permanent revolution, and it was the state ideology of the Soviet Union until the dissolution of 1991.

Its record in power is disputed: it brought rapid industrialisation, mass education and welfare, and also purges, labour camps and famines, and scholars disagree on how far the ideology itself explains the repression.
dyk: In 1934 Karl Radek proposed the name Marxism–Leninism–Stalinism in Pravda, but the name did not catch on, since Stalin and the party's ideologists preferred to keep Marxism–Leninism.
ev: The Bolsheviks seize power in the October Revolution and form the Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic
Stalin's Concerning Questions of Leninism presents Marxism–Leninism as a separate communist ideology
The first five-year plan begins the rapid industrialisation and collectivisation of the Soviet Union
The Great Purge begins, lasting until 1938; the Soviet Constitution of the same year is adopted
Mao Zedong establishes the People's Republic of China on 1 October after the Communist victory in the civil war
Khrushchev denounces Stalin's cult of personality at the 20th Congress of the Soviet party
Revolts across Central and Eastern Europe bring down the Eastern Bloc governments, while China's government ends protests by force at Tiananmen Square
Gorbachev announces the dissolution of the Soviet Union on 25 December

sections.origins:
Marxism–Leninism grew from the practice of the Bolshevik faction of the Russian Social Democratic Labour Party. Lenin made the Bolsheviks a vanguard of professional revolutionaries who practised democratic centralism, and he drew from the revolution of 1905 the conclusion that a small, disciplined party could sponsor a socialist revolution through agitation and propaganda. In Imperialism, the Highest Stage of Capitalism (1917) he argued that capitalist expansion led to colonial imperialism and to wars such as the Great War. The Bolsheviks seized power in the October Revolution of 1917, after the abdication of Nicholas II, and fought the Russian Civil War of 1917 to 1922.

The name and the doctrine came afterwards. After Lenin's death on 21 January 1924, Stalin, Kamenev and Zinoviev formed a troika against Trotsky, and the party chose Stalin's policy of socialism in one country over Trotsky's permanent revolution in 1925 and endorsed it in 1927. Stalin's Concerning Questions of Leninism (1926) represented Marxism–Leninism as a separate ideology with a global hierarchy of communist parties. Stalin's Dialectical and Historical Materialism became its foundation philosophy, and his 1938 textbook popularised it.
sections.ideas:
Marxism–Leninism holds that a two-stage communist revolution is needed to replace capitalism. A vanguard party, organised through democratic centralism, seizes power on behalf of the proletariat and founds a one-party state, which controls the means of production and suppresses the bourgeoisie and counter-revolution, in order to pave the way for a classless and stateless communist society. Its adherents treated class struggle as the dominating principle of social change and advocated a dictatorship of the proletariat. In the economy, scientific planning replaces market and price mechanisms, wages vary with skill and the intensity of work, and personal property that does not involve mass production stays outside state control.

It supports universal welfare, free education and health care, and the emancipation of women through secular marriage, easier divorce and the entry of women into industrial work. It aims at what its writers called the New Soviet man, a cultured citizen with proletarian class consciousness, and it is atheist, drawing on Hegel, Feuerbach, Marx and Lenin. In international relations it opposes colonialism and imperialism and supports anti-fascist popular fronts. Rachel Walker calls the term an empty one that is open to redefinition by each ruling party.
sections.spread:
Stalin's rise brought the Communist International under one orthodoxy by the late 1920s, and Marxist–Leninist parties led much of the armed resistance in the countries occupied by the Axis powers; in Yugoslavia the Partisans under Josip Broz Tito liberated territory and founded the communist state. After the Second World War the Soviet Union installed Marxist–Leninist governments in the Eastern Europe it had cleared of the Axis, and in 1949 Mao Zedong founded the People's Republic of China. Communists also took power in North Vietnam, Cuba, in the 1970s in Laos, Cambodia and a reunited Vietnam, and in African states including Angola, Mozambique and Ethiopia. South Yemen was the only openly communist state in the Arab world.

Variants split the movement. Stalin expelled Tito's Communist Party of Yugoslavia from the Cominform in 1948. After Khrushchev's denunciation of Stalin in 1956, Mao developed Maoism, and the Sino-Soviet split followed; Enver Hoxha then broke with China over its rapprochement with the United States and theorised Hoxhaism. Guevarism, Ho Chi Minh Thought and Juche, which replaced Marxism–Leninism in North Korea's constitution in 1992 and 2009, are other adaptations. Peru's Shining Path developed Marxism–Leninism–Maoism.
sections.power:
In the Soviet Union the five-year plans from 1928 brought rapid industrialisation and urbanisation, and collectivisation reached 98.0% of agriculture by 1941. The same rapid industrialisation also resulted in the Soviet famine of 1930 to 1933, which killed millions. Stalin dismantled party democracy and in the Great Purge of 1936 to 1938 had the NKVD arrest 1.5 million people in 1937 and 1938, of whom 681,692 were killed as enemies of the state. The Gulag held criminals, political dissidents, artists, intellectuals, homosexual people and religious opponents, and organised religion was repressed.

Elsewhere Marxist–Leninist rule had comparable features. The Great Leap Forward in China caused an estimated 15 to 55 million deaths between 1959 and 1961, mostly from starvation. The Khmer Rouge, a Maoist movement under Pol Pot, abolished money and private property and emptied Phnom Penh, and its Killing Fields caused the deaths of 2,700,000 people by mass murder and genocide. In Ethiopia the Derg's imposition of its radical ideas led to civil war. The Soviet Union intervened in Afghanistan in 1979 to establish a communist state. Defenders such as Michael Parenti stress economic, social and cultural rights, and Michael Ellman and Sen noted gains in health and life expectancy.
sections.critiques:
Critics from across the spectrum have attacked Marxism–Leninism, mainly in its Stalinist and Maoist forms. Daniel Gray, Silvio Pons and David Martin Walker hold that killings and repression, such as the Red Terror, the Great Purge and the Campaign to Suppress Counterrevolutionaries in China, came partly from the ideology, and Robert Service holds that atheism motivated mass religious persecution. Eric Voegelin called it inherently oppressive. Others reject such a link: Robert Vincent Daniels held that Marxism only justified Stalinism, Graeme Gill called Stalinism a sharp break from earlier developments, and Michael Geyer and Sheila Fitzpatrick criticised the totalitarian model for obscuring how the systems worked. Scholars disagree over the Holodomor as genocide, and Amartya Sen blamed the Great Chinese Famine on a lack of democracy.

From the left, Rosa Luxemburg predicted that banning multi-party democracy would turn the dictatorship of the proletariat into the dictatorship of a faction and then of an individual. Trotskyists described a degenerated workers' state under an unaccountable bureaucracy, and Raya Dunayevskaya and others called it state capitalism. Historiography is polarised too: Stéphane Courtois, Steven Rosefielde and Rudolph Rummel wrote of mass deaths as a direct consequence of the ideology, while Noam Chomsky, Kristen Ghodsee, Seumas Milne and Michael Parenti charged them with exaggeration.
sections.legacy:
Khrushchev's speech of 25 February 1956 began de-Stalinisation, the dismantling of the Gulag and the release of prisoners. In the 1980s Mikhail Gorbachev's perestroika and glasnost aimed at a return to a supposed ideal communist state, but the Solidarity union in Poland in 1980 had already shown resistance, and in 1989 revolts brought down the Eastern Bloc governments; Ceaușescu was overthrown and executed in Romania. Yugoslavia dissolved in 1992, and the Soviet Union ended when Gorbachev announced its dissolution on 25 December 1991.

Only a few parties kept power afterwards: China, Cuba, Laos and Vietnam hold Marxism–Leninism as their official ideology, although they interpret it differently. China under Deng Xiaoping reformed its economy while keeping one-party rule, and Xi Jinping has announced a deepening commitment to Marxism. In Russia the Communist Party of the Russian Federation won the 1995 legislative election. Parties such as AKEL in Cyprus, the Portuguese Communist Party and the Communist Party of India (Marxist) have taken part in governments or coalitions, while Maoist insurgencies continue in India, the Philippines and Turkey. Many historians and socialists dispute how faithful these movements were to the work of Karl Marx.

summary: Marxism–Leninism is the communist ideology formulated under Stalin after Lenin's death, built on a vanguard party, a one-party state and a planned economy. It was the state ideology of the Soviet Union and many other states, whose record of industrialisation, purges and famines is still disputed.
references: Robert Vincent Daniels, The Rise and Fall of Communism in Russia (Yale University Press, 2007)
Alfred B. Evans, Soviet Marxism-Leninism: The Decline of an Ideology (ABC-CLIO, 1993)
W. John Morgan, Marxism-Leninism: The Ideology of Twentieth-Century Communism (Elsevier, 2015)
Mark Sandle, A Short History of Soviet Socialism (UCL Press, 1999)
Robert Service, Comrades!: A History of World Communism (Harvard University Press, 2007)
notes: start 1924 (circa true): the article says it became a distinct movement after Lenin's death in 1924, and was first defined by Stalin 'in the 1920s'; Concerning Questions of Leninism is 1926.

Death tolls only as attributed: Great Leap Forward 'an estimated 15 to 55 million deaths between 1959 and 1961' (the Maoism article gives thirty million by some historians); Great Purge 1.5 million arrested and 681,692 killed in 1937-1938; Khmer Rouge 2,700,000. The Black Book of Communism's 93 or 100 million figure is left out.
The article calls the 1905 revolution the 'February Revolution of 1905' (wrongly); I wrote 'the revolution of 1905'.
Great Purge is dated 1936-1938 in the article but its NKVD arrest figures are for 1937-1938.

The article says Laos and Cambodia, Angola etc. became communist; I kept to the dated statements. 'In the 1970s' for Laos, Cambodia and Vietnam follows the article's 1976 reunification and 1975 Democratic Kampuchea; Laos is only named without a date.
The article says the Stalin-era Soviet Union 'inherited' labour camps from Nazi Germany (Service); an obvious slip, left out.
The article's 'Eastern Bloc' sentence on Khrushchev says he re-committed to permanent revolution; left out as contradictory with its other statements.

Left out: Quebec, Canada and Latin American episodes, Seychelles, Gambia, Burkina Faso, Moldova detail, the Marandici factors, the national party lists, the Korean War, the Pan-European Picnic, Hugo Chavez discussion.
